paper_a.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding (Devlin et al., 2018)

paper_b.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (Radford et al., 2018)

metadata.description: BERT and GPT-1 are concurrent (both 2018) approaches to pre-training Transformer models on unlabeled text for downstream NLP tasks. They share the same high-level paradigm (pre-train then fine-tune) but differ fundamentally in architecture and pre-training objective: GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer decoder with autoregressive language modeling; BERT uses a Transformer encoder with bidirectional masked language modeling. BERT's bidirectionality enables richer representations but prevents autoregressive generation.

matches.explanation: Both use multi-layer Transformer architectures with similar scale (BERT_BASE: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 110M params; GPT: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 117M params). The key difference: BERT uses the Transformer encoder (bidirectional self-attention); GPT uses the Transformer decoder (left-to-right causal self-attention).

Both define a self-supervised pre-training objective on unlabeled text, but they are fundamentally different. BERT: Masked Language Model (predict randomly masked tokens from bidirectional context). GPT: autoregressive LM (predict next token from left context only). MLM enables bidirectional conditioning but prevents generation; LM enables generation but is unidirectional. This is the core architectural distinction.

Both fine-tune all pre-trained parameters end-to-end on downstream tasks with a task-specific output layer. GPT adds an auxiliary LM loss ($\lambda L_1$) during fine-tuning; BERT does not. Both achieve strong downstream performance with minimal task-specific architecture changes.

Both convert diverse NLP tasks into a unified input format with special tokens. BERT: [CLS] + tokens + [SEP] + tokens + [SEP], with segment embeddings. GPT: [Start] + tokens + [Delim] + tokens + [Extract]. Functionally similar input engineering for the pre-train/fine-tune paradigm.
BERT's Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) objective is unique to BERT. GPT has no sentence-level pre-training objective. NSP was later shown to be of limited value (RoBERTa, 2019).

Both papers explicitly discuss the bidirectional vs. unidirectional distinction. BERT argues that bidirectional conditioning is crucial for understanding tasks. GPT's left-to-right design was motivated by enabling generation. BERT directly compares to and surpasses GPT on most benchmarks.
BERT's 80/10/10 masking strategy to mitigate the pre-train/fine-tune mismatch is specific to MLM. GPT has no such mismatch since the LM objective doesn't use special mask tokens.

Both report strong benchmark results. GPT: SOTA on 9/12 tasks, GLUE 72.8%. BERT: SOTA on 11 tasks, GLUE 80.5%, substantially surpassing GPT. BERT's bidirectional representations give a clear advantage on understanding tasks.
